planting.note: Plant container stock in fall or early spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in dappled shade to morning sun.

directions: Rufus is an early-generation Exbury hybrid deciduous azalea raised by Lionel de Rothschild's breeding program in Hampshire, England, prized for trusses of brilliant scarlet-red, trumpet-shaped flowers that open in mid-to-late spring on bare branches. Its saturated color made it a popular parent in later breeding programs seeking deep red tones in hardier, heat-tolerant azalea lines, including some American native hybrid crosses. Plant in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil with morning sun and afternoon shade, and mulch to keep the shallow root system cool. Prune only lightly right after flowering, since next year's buds set on the current season's growth soon after bloom ends.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; lutchuensis camellia is less cold-hardy than Camellia japonica and best suited to zones 8-10.

directions: Native to the Ryukyu Islands of southern Japan and Taiwan, this species camellia bears small, single, pure white flowers only an inch or so across, but they carry an unusually strong, sweet, jasmine-like fragrance rare among camellia species and cultivars alike. It flowers in late winter into early spring on a dense, twiggy, small-leaved evergreen shrub that stays more compact than Camellia japonica. Because true fragrance is so uncommon in the genus, breeders have used it extensively as a parent to introduce scent into modern hybrid camellias. Grow in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade with protection from hard freezes, since it is noticeably less cold-hardy than japonica or sasanqua types.

common_name: Hiawatha Azalea (Red Knap Hill Hybrid Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container stock in fall or early spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in dappled shade to morning sun.

directions: Hiawatha is a deciduous Knap Hill hybrid azalea from the English breeding line developed at the Knap Hill and Slocock nurseries in Surrey, valued for bold trusses of vivid red flowers that open in mid-spring on an upright, well-branched shrub. Like other Knap Hill selections, it combines showy, large-flowered trusses with good cold hardiness inherited from the group's mixed Asian and North American azalea species parentage. Its strong red color has made it a useful parent in later breeding programs crossing English hybrids onto native American azalea species for heat tolerance. Site in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil with dappled shade to morning sun, and avoid pruning in fall or winter since next year's flower buds are already set.

planting.note: Plant in fall or early spring; benefits from consistent moisture and acidic, well-drained soil while establishing.

directions: Desiree is an evergreen azalea from Ohio breeder Anthony Shammarello's cold-hardy hybrid line, developed specifically to extend reliable azalea flowering well north of the plant's traditional mild-winter range. It bears lavender-blue-toned pink, funnel-shaped flowers in a heavy spring flush on a compact, rounded, glossy-leaved mound. Shammarello crossed it with the Gable-bred 'Rosebud' to produce the later hybrid 'Elsie Lee,' passing on its cool lavender overtones to that cross. Grow in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade with some morning sun for best flower color, and prune only right after bloom since next year's buds set soon afterward.

planting.note: Plant container specimens in fall in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; this historic cultivar tolerates more heat, sun, and cold than bigleaf hydrangeas.

directions: Grandiflora is the historic nineteenth-century panicle hydrangea cultivar that gave rise to the common nickname 'PeeGee,' introduced to Western gardens from Japan in the 1860s and still grown well over a century later. It produces enormous, dense, cone-shaped flower panicles made up almost entirely of large sterile florets, opening creamy white in midsummer and aging through pink to parchment-bronze by fall, heavier and showier than the looser panicles of older European selections like 'Floribunda.' Left unpruned it grows into a large multi-stemmed shrub, or it can be trained with a single trunk into a small specimen tree. Because it blooms on new wood, prune hard in late winter to control size and encourage the largest flower heads.

planting.note: Plant grafted, container-grown trees in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in a sheltered, sunny site away from frost pockets, since the earliest flowers open before any protective leaf cover.

directions: Lanarth is a named clone of Magnolia campbellii var. mollicomata, the western Chinese botanical variety that flowers earlier and more reliably from a younger age than typical Campbell's magnolia. Selected and distributed from Lanarth, a historic garden estate in Cornwall, England, it is valued for intensely saturated rose-purple to magenta, goblet-shaped flowers up to 8 inches across that open on bare branches in late winter before any leaves emerge. Like other campbellii types, its early flowers are vulnerable to late frost damage, so a sheltered site away from cold air drainage is essential. Given room to mature over decades, it becomes an outsized specimen tree valued by magnolia collectors for its exceptionally deep flower color.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

common_name: Robusta Sargent Magnolia (Large-Flowered Chinese Magnolia Variety)

planting.note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in a sheltered site away from frost pockets, since the earliest flowers open well before any leaf cover.

directions: Native to the mountains of Sichuan, China, this larger-flowered botanical variety of Sargent's magnolia bears huge, pendulous, rose-pink flowers up to 10 inches across that hang bell-like from bare branches in late winter to early spring, ahead of the emerging leaves. Its flowers are noticeably larger and more substantial than the typical species form, making it a favorite of collectors and a frequent parent in breeding programs seeking size and early bloom in hybrid magnolias. The tree eventually becomes massive given many decades in the ground, so it needs a spacious site away from frost pockets that could damage its earliest flowers. Grow in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun with some wind shelter.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)
